utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the accused into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-03-67-PT, the Prosecution versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today, Wednesday, the 4th of April, 2007, I'd like to greet the Prosecution, Mr. Seselj who has just entered the courtroom, and everyone else assisting us in our work, in particular the registrar, the usher, and everyone else in and around the courtroom. This is the second Status Conference since we met three weeks ago, and I said on that occasion that we would have a meeting every two or three weeks to prepare for the beginning of the trial in the best possible conditions. In the court, this hearing in the presence of the Prosecution and Mr. Seselj, I intend to deal with all the pending motions, to take stock of these motions, and this concerns in particular the problem of translation and the responses of the parties concerned. But, first of all, I would like to remind everyone of the fact that the main purpose of a Status Conference is to allow the parties to communicate as best as possible, in particular with regard to exhibits. And Judge, the Pre-Trial Judge, must also ensure that the dialogue between the parties, the Prosecution and the accused, runs as smoothly as possible. My main concern is, therefore, to establish a permanent and fruitful dialogue between the parties concerned. I will now inform the parties, the Prosecution and Mr. Seselj, of the administrative situation as far as the Trial Chamber is concerned. First of all, I would like to inform Mr. Seselj of the following, because there was a minor error in the motion that concerns contempt of court. The President of the Chamber and Judge Robinson -- I'm just the Pre-Trial Judge, and the third Judge is Judge Bonomy. This case has been assigned to Trial Chamber III which is presided by Judge Robinson, which means that in all the documents, all the motions must have in the heading Judge Robinson as the Presiding Judge. I am just the Pre-Trial Judge. The last Status Conference, I informed Mr. Seselj that I was going to contact the President to deal with appointing the Chamber that will be responsible for the Seselj case. For the moment, no decision has been taken. So I'm not in a position to inform Mr. Seselj which Trial Chamber will be dealing with his case, since this is a matter for the President of the Tribunal to decide. He designates the Judges who will take part in the trial. As everyone is well aware, there are three Trial Chambers in this Tribunal: Trial Chamber I, Trial Chamber II, and Trial Chamber III. They are first-level Trial Chambers, and they deal with cases that are assigned to them. They deal with the trials assigned to them. But given the completion strategy and the need to complete the Tribunal's work as expeditiously as possible, given the need to put all the accused on trial expeditiously, ad hoc Trial Chambers may have to be established that include Judges that are part of or members of other Trial Chambers. As a general rule, a Trial Chamber is composed of a Permanent Judge and of Ad Litem Judges; there can be a Permanent Judge and two Ad Litem Judges, or two Permanent Judges and one Ad Litem Judge, or we can have three Permanent Judges, but it's for the President of the Tribunal to decide on such matters, on the composition of Trial Chambers. At present, I'm not in a position to tell you, Mr. Seselj, anything about the composition of the Trial Chamber that will be responsible for your case. And the second administrative matter I want to deal with and that I would like to inform you of is the following: When there is a trial, a trial requires a lot of administrative staff members: The registrar is responsible for the exhibits of the case; it requires an usher, who brings the witnesses into the courtroom; and the trial also requires interpreters, as we are working in three languages: your own, English, and French, it is necessary to have interpreters. And we also need security officers, which means that a trial requires administrative staff, but that's not the only thing. The Judges require assistants to help them with their work, and they also need the assistance of secretaries. As far as assistants are concerned, the procedure in a trial is as follows: There's a P5 assistant, who is the Legal Officer responsible for the assistants; and below that person there is a P4 Legal Officer; and there is the Trial Chamber's Legal Officer, whose grade is P3; and the Judges have an assistant, whose grade is P2 as well. All trials are automatically composed of such staff members. Since I've been designated to be a member of Trial Chamber III, I only have one assistant who's currently for me and assisting me; I have no one else. And that, Mr. Seselj, means that once the Chamber has been finally composed, all these assistants will be designated; for the moment, that is not the case. In addition, as you are well aware, we have three courtrooms in this Tribunal. Today, we are in Courtroom I. We also have Courtroom II and Courtroom III. These courtrooms are constantly functioning. This morning in this courtroom, there was a hearing, an appeals hearing, and this afternoon there will be another trial. So all the courtrooms are fully occupied. And this means that there is an annual plan that is established for the trials that are ongoing. At the moment, there are three Chambers dealing with six trials because there are hearings in the morning and then in the afternoon. And the Tribunal is working even more intensively since -- or will be working even more intensively since the seventh trial is being prepared. Yours or your trial will be added to this total number of trials; that means eight trials, we will have eight trials, and we have three courtrooms, and this will make it necessary to adapt and manage the work of the Tribunal so that we can deal with eight trials in three courtrooms. I have spoken to the Registrar, who is the administrative individual responsible for all such matters, and I will convey to you what the Registrar told me. We have budgetary rules that make it possible to fund the personnel, the trials, and I believe that funds have been provided for six trials, not for eight. This causes a problem. How can we finance eight trials, given that the budget we have at our disposal is a budget for six trials? Naturally, it might always be possible to ask everyone to make additional efforts. I myself, as I told you last time, I myself am involved in another trial. This afternoon, I will be sitting in another trial, so one can also ask Judges to work more. We can ask their assistants to work around-the-clock. All such things are possible. Everything is possible, but at one point in time the funds will be exhausted, and in that case we'll run into serious problems. I would, nevertheless, like to re-assure you and tell you that the Registrar said that he would do his utmost to deal with these problems. And I believe that we will all do everything we can to ensure the expeditious commencement of your trial in the best possible conditions. So I wanted to explain all of these matters to you for you to be aware of the fact that a trial requires certain logistics, administrative logistics. A minute ago, I mentioned interpretation. Interpretation is a subject that I have to address with you, Mr. Seselj. I need to draw your attention to the fact that from time to time, there might be some errors with regard to what has actually been said by all the parties involved. Recently I was informed of the fact that here we have the benefit of simultaneous interpretation; whereas, there are other procedures that can be followed. For example, interpretation can also be consecutive. As you can see, what is being said here appears instantaneously on the screen that you have before you at this speed and the fact that the interpretation is simultaneous, according to very qualified individuals, means that there can be a 20 per cent margin of error when it comes to simultaneous interpretation. This also concerns the sense of what is said -- in fact, as far as the sense is concerned, there is a 10 per cent margin of error, and this margin of error or these errors can be corrected in two ways. We can follow the English version on the monitor, and if we understand French or your language, corrections can be made; but as you will be defending yourself and if you're not assisted by anyone, you won't be focused or you won't be completely focused on the screen. When I speak to you, I don't follow what appears on the screen at the same time. If we subsequently discover that what you said was erroneously interpreted or interpreted in a rough manner, you can always say, Well, I said such and such a thing, and I wanted to point out the fact that the English word doesn't correctly reflect what I actually said. So you always have the possibility of correcting such errors, but I wanted to draw your attention to this factor, this difficulty. I have also noticed that when I listen to answers of questions put to a witness -- well, I can't always follow the interpretation. I wanted to point out the fact that sometimes there can be problems when it comes to interpretation, but it's always possible to correct any errors made later on. So, Mr. Seselj, before we deal with the subject of motions, I'd like to say something else about administrative matters in conclusion. The Registrar has provided me with information about the facilities that you have at your disposal. The Registrar has informed me of the following, and you will tell me whether this is correct or whether anything needs to be clarified or corrected. As far as administrative matters are concerned, I'll now tell you about what has been done to make sure that you can defend yourself under the best possible conditions. You have a special cell for your confidential files, and this cell could also be used by you as an office. You have a telephone line and a telecopier so that communications will be protected by professional secret. I have also been told that in the penitentiary area, you have a room reserved for meetings that you will have with your legal advisors and with the assistant that will be entrusted with the case. The jurisprudence of the Tribunal is at your disposal in your own language. The administration have provided you with a computer and a CD and DVD device, as well as technical assistance for the use of those instruments, but apparently you have refused these devices. The administration is suggesting some basic training for the use of the e-court system for your legal assistants, because there is an e-court system which requires some knowledge of the system, and the administration is ready to train your legal advisors in its use. You may also obtain all the video-recordings of the hearings through the assistance of the department for judicial assistance, and you will be able to have a recorder so as to review all the hearings, and the administration will provide you with all the necessary equipment. The administration has also proposed a liaison officer for you, but apparently you didn't want one. The administration tells me that a monthly allowance had been envisaged for the assistant entrusted with the case to help you with the preparations, to act as an intermediary between you and the administration, et cetera, et cetera. The administration have also informed me that they are in the process of assigning your legal advisors; therefore, from the point of view of the administration, the relationship between you are protected by confidential -- professional confidentiality. Therefore, your assistants, being familiar with the confidential documents, are obliged to respect this confidentiality. Furthermore, I have been told that your assistants, when they come to The Hague, their travelling expenses will be covered by the Tribunal once per month. And to allow your advisors and the assistant to help you in the most effective manner, an apartment will also be provided and the costs covered by the Tribunal. Finally, I have been told that all these facilities envisaged by the Statute go beyond those that Mr. Slobodan Milosevic had at his disposal, who, like you, provided his own defence. So that would be the situation with regard to the position of the administration with respect to the facilities which have been put at your disposal for your defence. In the list I have gone through, there are two that you didn't want. Perhaps you will tell me the reasons why, because I am totally unaware of those reasons. This is what I wanted to say as a preliminary introduction before we actually undertake the examination of various pending motions to see where we stand with them and to discuss the various problems. So at this stage, Mr. Seselj, I give you the floor, if you wish to comment on the points that I have just covered so that I can hear your views and we can find out the points of disagreement and the points with which you are satisfied. So I give you the floor, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Antonetti, first of all, I should like to comment on the question of simultaneous interpretation, which you have highlighted. Four years ago, I raised this problem at a Status Conference, in view of the fact that at The Hague Tribunal when talking about the total number of staff members from the territory of the former Yugoslavia, a very large number of them are of Croatian ethnicity, and this wouldn't bother me when it comes to interpreters, if some of them did not frequently use newly fabricated words. You know, Mr. Antonetti, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims all speak Serbian, the Serbian language. The Croats accepted the Serbian language 150 years ago because they didn't have their own literary language, so they neglected their own Kajkavian and Ekavian, which they took over from the Slovenes. What happened then was that Croats started making up new words so that their language should artificially be differentiated from Serbian, and that is the only thing I am bothered by when I hear a new word that I never heard of before. This is not the case with the interpreter I am listening to just now. I have noticed that she is Croat, but she's interpreting quite correctly and I haven't noticed that she used any such invented words. But there are some who do this on purpose, and often this can be irritating, and especially in some cases I don't even know their meaning if they were made up only a couple of days ago. So this is a problem that should be borne in mind. It can be resolved but with instructions to the interpreters not to use newly compiled words, not a word that wasn't in the dictionary 20 or 30 years ago and especially not a word that was made up after the dissolution of Yugoslavia. Those are words that I simply do not know. 90 per cent of Croats themselves are unable to use them, and at least 50 per cent don't understand them. I have been given a protection by decision of a Trial Chamber, and that is that after every Status Conference, I get a video-recording of that conference. This is to check what I myself have said and the witnesses who may be testifying, who will mostly be speaking in Serbian. So the problem is that your transcripts are English or French. So what is necessary is for those transcripts to be reviewed and checked after the hearings. I'm unable to follow the English transcripts in the courtroom. My knowledge of English is not sufficient for me to be able to rely on it, nor can I because I have to concentrate in another direction. But in any event, what I receive on a video-recording, my legal advisors will take down on paper and then I can use it, and I can intervene later on if somebody is incorrectly quoting in another document. So that is a guarantee of some sort that I have. Those recordings of Status Conferences would be given to me immediately the next day - that was the decision - but it took a whole week for me to receive the recording from the last Status Conference, and I had to address a special request to remind them. But also, it was the first time that the last Status Conference was not broadcast on the internet because my assistants could follow on the internet, and then they could take it down on paper even before they receive my videotapes from me. The last Status Conference for vague reasons and incomprehensible reasons were not broadcast. I can make my own speculations as to why that is so, but I'll avoid -- refrain from doing that. What the Registrar has informed you of with respect to the facilities for my defence is partially true. I have been -- I have received promises from the director, and I believe that he will fulfil those promises, that I will have a telephone, a fax machine, a photocopying machine, and that I will have another cell as an extension to my own. It is simple to break -- to make a door in the partitioning wall so that these two cells would be connected. If they're not connected, then whenever I need to go to the cell with the documents, I have to look for the guard to unlock it. I got up today at 4.00. I usually get up between 4.00 and 5.00 a.m., that is when I work best; however, those cells are unlocked at 7.00 a.m. But you know when you're an intellectual and when an idea occurs to you if you're able to work on it straight away, you can do so; but if you have to look for the guard and to ask him to unlock the door, the idea may evaporate. And I do hope that the warden will fulfil his promises, and then I can use the offices that are used by any other attorneys when consulting with their clients. I do not insist that this should be just my own room if I am given this extended cell for my documents. The jurisdiction was never given to me. I have managed to get only the first-instance and second-instance judgements, though some have still not reached me even though they were handed down several months ago, probably it's due to the translation problems. I have asked for the entire case law, the pre-trial decisions and rulings, the appeals, rulings, and et cetera. But the registry has regularly refused to give me this. I have also asked to be given in Serbian the decision of the International Court regarding Rwanda because the Judges have frequently referred to that case, especially in footnotes. The Registrar refused this, and the Pre-Trial Judge said I had no right to have this, and I had to find the funds to pay translators in Belgrade to translate the judgements of The International Court for Rwanda, which for me were important so as to be able to respond to the submissions of the Prosecution. You know, Mr. Antonetti, that the International Court for Yugoslavia and the one for Rwanda are closely linked, not by the nature of their work, but they are organically linked because for a long time they had a single Appeals Chamber. The Appeals Chamber for Yugoslavia was also the Appeals Chamber of the International Court for Rwanda, and it was the duty of the Registrar to provide me with the translations of all their judgements. They would not translate the judgements for the Albanians, so that I had to have them translated myself; that is, to pay for their translation in Belgrade. That is the Musliu and Limaj case and Beqa Beqaj case. We have had two cases so far. So these are problems involving a great deal of money and a lot of work, and the Registrar should have done all this because the entire case law of this Tribunal should exist in the Serbian language, of course in French and in English, because all the people involved in the conflict in Yugoslavia, with the exception of the Albanians, spoke Serbo-Croatian regardless of how they call it. Some call it Croatian; some Bosnian, a language that never existed; some are now calling it Montenegrin, but according to linguistics, it is all one and the same language, the Serbian language. I have been offered a computer and a DVD; I refused those, first of all because I don't know how to use a computer, and I never had any necessity to learn. I used to be able to play a game of chess on the computer, but for my legal work I had no need because I had a secretary who would do that instead of me. So why should I spend time to gain knowledge of this equipment when I have someone else to do it for me? As for the DVD, I really don't need one. Why? Because when the Prosecution gives transcripts from other trials in the file, they do so on paper when they provide those documents to you, usually in English. And what they would do for me would be on a computer disk, and then I would have to listen to this. This would require an enormous amount of time; whereas, 90 per cent of that time would be wasted. This must be on paper because if it is on paper, then I can leaf through the document and focus on the essential points. If I receive this on diskette, then I literally have to listen to everything in the slow way in which it is done in the courtroom. This is, in a sense, preventing the accused to defend himself. With regard to some disks that I was offered - I think I said this on the 3rd of November at a Status Conference - I said that I would need 400 days to hear all those disks if I were to work eight hours a day, and that is simply impossible. Everything has to be on paper and only on paper is this valid for me as a document because documents have to be on paper by definition. A computer is a technical appliance, as are the disks, and scanning of documents, et cetera. But unless something is on paper, it doesn't exist as a document. And if it's not on paper, I can't use it in the preparation of my defence. As far as my legal assistants are concerned, I appreciate the Registrar's concern to train them, to ensure that they are capable of having access to the electronic database so that they can find documents in the courtroom, documents that are needed very rapidly. But you know their status hasn't yet been regulated. Only one thing has been dealt with, and that's the fact that their appointment as my legal assistants has been accepted, but they are professionally involved in Belgrade, and they work in Belgrade for me during their free time, after their work. In order for them to come to The Hague, they have to resign from their posts in Belgrade. And they then have to commit themselves to my defence alone, and in that case they should be adequately paid on a monthly basis. The Registrar persists in refusing to accept this. I recently had three conversations with John Hocking, the Deputy Registrar. We addressed all these matters, but we have failed to find a common understanding so far. The registry refused to accept the fact that it's their duty to finance my defence according to the Statute. He says that is the case only if counsel is assigned to me, but that's not what the Statute says, that's not the only way my defence can be funded. I can't give up my fundamental right to defence myself because the registry blackmails me and says that only if I have assigned counsel will the defence be financed. I'm saying I'm not going to make too many requests. If they don't want to pay for my defence, I'll just appear in the courtroom and defend myself. But then I'll be alone in the courtroom, no one will be with me in The Hague, no one will come to see me, perhaps I'll have some telephone conversations with people who might help me from Belgrade. They've said that I've been granted more facilities than Slobodan Milosevic had been granted. Well, what have they granted me? Once a month, they'll pay for an invited to come to The Hague. They'll pay 1.500 euros to the case manager, and they'll provide me with a flat that's worth 1.200 euros a month. And that's quite true, Mr. Milosevic didn't have such facilities, but I'd like to remind you of the fact that Mr. Milosevic never raised the issue of the finance of his defence and he didn't request funds for his defence. He didn't ask for anything and they didn't give him anything. He never wanted to write a single written submission. He was consistent in his position that the Tribunal was illegitimate. My position is somewhat different. I dispute the legality of the court, but I have to accept the physical existence of this Tribunal. I will still bring into question the legality of this court, but I will use everything that I -- all the means I can to defend myself, even if the Tribunal is not a legitimate one. So my position is significantly different from that of Mr. Milosevic and comparison is out of place. In this case, as far as -- as far as a liaison officer is concerned, I don't see what his role would be. I just need someone from the registry to provide documents. So far this hasn't been done. I was provided with the amended Rules very belatedly. I don't know when these Rules were last amended. The last amendment I have is dated the 13th of September. Perhaps it was amended after that date, but I always received the amended Rules several months late. Sometimes I received the amended rules in Serbian after three or four amendments had been made. The registry should have records showing when I was provided with a given version of the Rules, and then this matter will be clear. Because since I have been here, there have been 16 amendments of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and only on five or six occasions was I provided with the new amended version of the Rules. So you can see for yourself how conscientiously they performed their duties. As far as an agreement with my legal officers are concerned, it will be signed once I have the text of the agreement in the Serbian language. My legal advisors have been shown that text or were shown that text in English in December, and they couldn't sign the text without my agreement, and I am requesting that I first be provided with it in the Serbian language, and then I can authorise them to sign it. The registry is still waiting, and they tell you that they are ready to sign. They are far from ready to sign until I'm provided with this in the Serbian language, and until I tell my legal advisors that they can sign it. How am I to know what they will be signing for the moment? The legal advisors have been allowed to come once a month. One legal advisor every month. Second one, second month, and then the third one on the third month, and then it's impossible to work systematically with these advisors. And so I told them, all three of you will come once every three months. John Hocking, at the last meeting said -- or, rather, promised he would consider the issue and perhaps allow the three of them to come once a month, but this has not yet been decided on. As far as these legal advisors are concerned, they have to be professionally engaged in my case, which means that the registry has to assess on the basis of all the relevant information how much my defence will cost in the pre-trial phase, in the trial phase while the Prosecution calls its witnesses, when the defence calls its witnesses, and during the appeals stage, and then they should say this is the total cost for the defence, this is how much I can pay. I provided them with information of my own property. They said I didn't want to cooperate. I can't cooperate if the members of my -- or if my close family or distant family members don't want to speak to investigators from the registry, a certain Jovanovic appeared, a Slovenian, who has origins in Valjevo. He arrived at the gate to my house. My wife saw him from the balcony, told him she thought he was disgusting and wouldn't let him enter the house. My mother didn't want to speak to him. She said she didn't participate in any crimes I may have committed, and she didn't want to suffer the consequences. But what is a fact is that from the time these alleged crimes were committed, I didn't transfer any property to anyone else, to members of my family, et cetera. So how can one talk about a lack of cooperation? I am cooperating. I said I had $70.000 in a bank in New York, and you know what the consequences were? Someone from this Tribunal ordered that that money should be blocked. I contacted the Serbian consul in The Hague, he had contact with the American consulate, and he received in writing information according to what someone had decided that that money over there should be frozen and that all transactions had been banned unless it concerned paying some American lawyer I might engage in order to defend me before this Tribunal. Naturally, I would rather lose that money than accept such blackmail. That money has been in the account since 1989. It was honestly won. It was before the war. I'm not a refugee from The Hague Tribunal. I'm not fleeing from The Hague Tribunal, and I was prepared to use that money. This money should be transferred to Belgrade and then the registry can say, Well, $70.000, that's the amount I'll give to participate in my defence and the outstanding amount will be covered by the registry. I'm not asking for the registry to pay money into my account, but they should assess the cost of the defence and they should say the main legal advisors, Zoran Tasic has such and such an amount, or I should provide a list of 25 or 27 individuals and say such and such an individual costs such and such an amount, these are their accounts, pay it. But the registry refuses to consider paying for such defence. They don't want to do that. I've continued to raise this issue, but even without such funds I'll defend myself. But, Mr. Antonetti, you know that this trial cannot be a fair trial if I do not have the adequate funds at my disposal for my defence. What are the correct criteria of which you use to assess the costs? I made three requests. Firstly, that the registry should make public how much money was paid to Aleksandar Lazarevic, the first stand-by lawyer. Van der Spoel, the second stand-by lawyer and his team because he formed an entire team in agreement with the registry. How much money did Cooper and his team had been paid? This was all in the pre-trial phase. This could provide certain guide-lines but they're keeping this as kept a a secret. UN funds can't be kept secret, this has to be made public, and I will not cease to make a request for this to be made public. And my second request is that I should be provided with information as to the costs of the defence in all the other cases financed by the International Tribunal. My case is a third-category case. It's the most difficult case. My crimes are the most widespread crimes. Everyone else has been charged with crimes in one or two states, I've been charged with crimes in three states. That's the most complicated case. So let's see what the objective criteria are. A new crime has been invented in my case, a crime that never existed before in international law, a hate speech. So it's not incitement to commit crimes. There's public and direct incitement, incitement to loot, rape, et cetera, or encouraging perpetrators to perpetrate certain crimes through acts or omissions, but my passionate speeches are supposed to have incited the desire in others to kill or to rape. So this is what such hatred speech is supposed to mean. This also has an effect on the funds I need for my defence. I have to engage lawyers throughout the world. For example, Jacques Verges, the well-known French lawyer; lawyer Levy; Noam Chomsky, et cetera, et cetera. Because these incredible things in my indictment has to be analysed into its component parts, and I have been preparing myself psychologically and in professional terms as well. Without professional assistance, it's probably impossible for me to analyse all these matters. This is the main problem that has to be dealt with here. My third request was that the Prosecution should provide information as to how much money they spent in my case for investigators, for administration, for typists. This would also indicate certain things. Don't misunderstand me. I'm not asking that the same amount be spent on my defence as was spent on the Prosecution when they were preparing the indictment against me, but there should be some sort of ratio. Perhaps they are more greedy, perhaps they like spending more, they like money more, et cetera, et cetera. I understand all of that, but that is an indication of the cost of my defence, if taken together with other indicia. I want to compare my case to the cost of the defence in other cases; for example, in the Krajisnik case, in the Seferovic case -- I apologise in the Sefer Halilovic case, and in other cases that have been brought before this Tribunal, so that we can see what the situation is. And I am saying this openly and I am using facts, but they are keeping all of these matters secret, and they don't respond. It's futile for me to write hundreds of submissions, and they remain silent and they repeat the same story. They say I don't have such rights, and in my opinion I have such rights. If you come to the conclusion that I don't have the right to have my defence financed, I'll agree. I'll accept that I should sit here on my own, and that I should defend myself without the assistance of anyone. If that is how you would like things to work, if that's the procedure you would like us to follow, I'll accept that procedure and then we can start with the trial tomorrow. I will do nothing to postpone the beginning of the trial. I haven't done anything to do that to date, but I'm fighting for my procedural rights to the extent that I'm capable of doing that and in a way that was not pleasant for the registry and the previous Pre-Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this stage, does the Prosecution wish to intervene regarding various points raised by Mr. Seselj? And I wish to say that I myself will make a few points of clarification regarding a certain number of points raised. Mr. Saxon, do you wish to intervene?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At this point, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have said a number of things, and as a Pre-Trial Judge, I will respond to them but without speaking on behalf of the Chamber but only in my own name within the framework of the authority vested in me by the Rules. Regarding the questions of interpretation, you noted that certain new terms have been introduced, specifically by Croat interpreters. This is something I was totally unaware of. I will certainly ask the service in charge of the interpretation to tell me what their position is, and I have taken note of this point which you have drawn my attention to. Concerning the numerous motions and requests that you have made with respect to the registry and to which you have not received replies, according to you, you have asked to be informed of the amount spent for certain trials and you named those trials. I personally don't know why the registry has not responded - that is their responsibility - but only with regard to the documents that are available to all regarding the financing of the Tribunal. As you know, the UN General Assembly determines the budget, and there are documents that are available to see the various items in the budget. And on that basis you can gain information. This may not be quite precise, regarding the distribution among the various trials, and I quite understand that. But this is a question of your relationship with the registry, and this is not something I can deal with. It is their responsibility and not mine if they do not reply to your request. You also touched upon another point and that is the question of remuneration of your assistants. You already said last time, and I understood, that the three assistants were deputies in parliament in Belgrade just now, and that they were waiting to learn how they would be engaged here, so as to resign their positions there and come to your assistance. You have told me just now that there is an agreement that is about to be finalised but which has still not been translated into your language, which is delaying things. Regarding this financial aspect, the registry has told me the following, the Registrar, and I personally have no response to give you. The legal position is the following: Pursuant to Article 24(D) of the Statute -- 21(4)(d) of the Statute, the accused has the right to have a Defence counsel of his choice, a counsel assigned to him, or the appointment of counsel if he has not -- doesn't have the funds to pay. And the Tribunal relies on the provisions of 21(4)(d) of the Statute. Again, the Registrar says: In order to benefit from such aid, the accused must request the appointment of an assigned counsel and demonstrate that he is partially indigent. In view of this position of the Registrar and your position, I note that there is, indeed, a problem there, which still has not been regulated. I hope that the Registrar will find a solution. I have had several working meetings with him, and for him to find a solution to this legal problem between the Statute and the budgetary rules, he may have a solution, and that would be to consult the legal counsel in the UN to see whether this interpretation of aid can be interpreted in such a way that your assistants' costs should be remunerated and covered. This is a budgetary issue which really is quite beyond me, but I note on the basis of what you have told me that, for the present, this question has not been regulated at all. You have also raised another point which was of interest to me, because I quite agree with you, and that is the question of documents. Like you, I believe that in order to work well, one must have documents in paper, hard copy documents, not in electronic form. You have explained why, and like you I am in agreement with you because I also can only work on the basis of documents. As a jurist, the use of documents with the help of computers is for me difficult. It does not allow one to work under the best conditions. Therefore, on this point I agree with you. But I wish to underline that I am a member of a Trial Chamber and that my colleagues may not agree with me. But as far as I am concerned, in my personal opinion, I believe that one should be able to work on the basis of documents. And I will be coming back to that in a moment when we examine the question of motions. You have also indicated something which seems to me to be common sense, and that is a question of two cells that should be connected so as to allow you to consult your documents whenever you need to do so without looking for a guard to unlock the cell. This seems to me quite logical that this should be done, the more so that you told me that it was done in the case of Mr. Milosevic. So there's no reason why you should not have two connected cells so that you can move from one to another to work when you like. As you have said, you like to work from 4.00 a.m., and I don't think that this should be a problem. This can be resolved very quickly. Last time, also, I told you that I personally intend to go to visit the conditions that are available to you for preparing your defence and the facilities that are made available to you in the Detention Unit. Before touching upon the motions now, I should very briefly like to cover what we are duty-bound to do at a Status Conference, and that is the question of your state of health. And according to what the doctor has told me, there are no particular problems which would prevent your presence at trial, and therefore I have received a medical report, a detailed one, dated the 13th of March, 2007, which tells me that you are able to follow the proceedings without any problem. Concerning now the issue of motions. There are two sources: There are yours and those of the Prosecution. Let us first examine your own motions. First of all, there is motion number 250 concerning a request for an inquiry into the question of contempt of court. The Prosecution has to respond, and now I turn to Mr. Saxon to see when the Prosecution will file a response to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Saxon, we're not touching upon the content. I'm just asking you the date when you will respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, we're having a technical problem right now. Could the Legal Officer perhaps tell us the date when this motion was filed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The motion by Mr. Seselj is dated the 8th of March, 2007. It's a motion that was registered with the registry on the 23rd of March. So the motion was drafted in his language on the 8th of March; then it was sent to the translation service, and it was translated into English and registered on the 23rd of March. I have a reference number here D17364. And according to the Rules, you have 14 days to respond and that would -- that deadline would expire on the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask for an extension of time until Tuesday of next week to respond, because I have asked the investigators in my office, who were mentioned in this motion, to review their records that are related to the allegations, and as some of these allegations relate to events that go back years, I would ask to have until Tuesday of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So I can grant you an extension so that you may respond. Once this response has been registered, together with my colleagues in Chamber III, we will make our decision with respect to that motion. That is one motion which is currently pending. There's also a motion filed by Mr. Seselj, the number is 240, filed on the 11th of January, 2007, and this motion is addressed -- addressed to the Chamber, asks the Chamber to order the Prosecution to convey to the accused several filings with regard to several persons. It relates mainly to experts. I have been told that Mr. Seselj should have received these documents on the 13th of February. Mr. Seselj, have you received a response to your request? Because I have been told that you should have received a reply on the 13th of February.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not true, what the Prosecution says, Mr. Antonetti. I asked to be given the expert reports in paper and in the Serbian language, which the Prosecution tried to hand over to me in electronic form in -- last summer, sometime in July. Instead of that, the Prosecution has now given me only their introductory filings, with an indication that the expert report can be found on DVD such and such. I have not received those expert reports of Davor Strinovic, Zoran Stankovic, Ewa Tabeau, and Ivan Grujic. This was on the 12th, 13th, and 14th of July last year that an attempt was made to give me these reports in the form of diskettes, and the responses reached me on the 9th of February in the form of just the introduction written by the Prosecution saying that the diskettes are the reports. So, according to my records, it was not the 12th of February, but the 19th of -- the 9th of February, I'm sorry. If it is up to the Prosecution to respond on my submissions on a special defence, then I have received their response, so I am not sure what specifically this relates to. I have received this, but I can only comment on it because I absolutely disagree with them. It is very superficial; they have translated only two. Sometimes they have done summaries, sometimes there are no summaries even, and this is absolutely unacceptable for a serious discussion, because in those 15 documents on special defence, I intend to examine many Prosecution experts and I will also be examining Defence experts on these issues as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I believe I've identified the problem, and I believe that the Prosecution agrees with you. The Prosecution sent you the documents on disk. Is that correct, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In general, yes, Your Honour. But I must make one comment to flesh-out the information that is available to the Chamber, if you allow me, and this is a matter that the Prosecution wanted to raise today anyway. The Prosecution is concerned about the status of materials that were disclosed to assigned Defence counsel between last summer and December of 2006, and the Prosecution believes that the materials that Mr. Seselj has been discussing during the last few minutes fall within this category. And the Prosecution would respectfully ask that perhaps the Chamber, with the help of the registry to clarify this situation, will this material that was provided to the then-assigned Defence counsel be provided to the accused? From the Prosecution's point of view, obviously that would be an efficient way of addressing this problem, but we will leave that to the Chamber and the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Saxon. You've put your finger on a problem that has not yet been addressed; namely, certain documents were directly addressed to lawyers designated by the previous Chamber, and we don't know what these lawyers did. What should they do? Theoretically, they should return these documents to the registry, who should then provide the Prosecution with the documents, who should then provide Mr. Seselj with the documents. That's the procedure, same as for the transcript, and I would like to ask the registry to do what is necessary to deal with this matter, to deal with the documents provided to the previous counsel. And naturally, these documents should be returned, given the situation that we now find ourselves in and the fact that Mr. Seselj is defending himself. But there is another problem that I should inform the parties of. As far as electronic disclosure is concerned, last time I addressed the issue, but I have to return to the subject now. Trial Chamber I, the previous Trial Chamber, handed down a decision on the 4th of July, 2006, according to which there should be electronic disclosure. This decision is a decision that Mr. Seselj had filed an appeal against, and the Appeals Chamber has to rule on the appeal because before it rules on the appeal, no one can move forward. So the situation is frozen for the moment. Mr. Seselj can't see these documents that were disclosed to him electronically, and the Prosecution, basing itself on the 4th of July, 2006 decision maintains its position. So it's now for the Appeals Chamber to decide. That is the only solution to the matter. We can now move on to examining other motions. Mr. Saxon, yes, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly, just one more point of information that I would like to bring to the Chamber's attention. The Prosecution has been informed that with respect to the materials that were provided to the assigned Defence counsel during 2006, the Prosecution is informed that the registry attempted to provide these materials to the accused in February of this year, and the accused refused to accept them. That's all I wanted you to know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I assume that they were provided in electronic form. So that's the same problem. Would you confirm that, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Antonetti, I received the letter from the registry, in which they informed me of the fact that there were 40 parcels of documents. Not binders, I'm talking about boxes. These are documents gathered by Hooper and his team, and they assumed that the documents among them that they received from the Prosecution and also that they were confidential documents that they were preparing for my supposed defence. I'm not at all interested in them. Secondly, I assume that all the documents they received from the Prosecution are documents in English. A while ago, you were quite correct in saying which method we should follow. I never accepted Hooper as my counsel, and I don't want to receive anything from him. But the registry has to return this to the Prosecution, and the Prosecution has to provide me with the documents in a correct manner. I never refused to take over any documents if it was in a hard copy and in the Serbian language. The Prosecution confirmed that. And what should I do? I'm not someone to inherit Cooper's matters. I'm not someone who can say that he acted in my case in a legal manner either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record at least some of the documents that were offered to be provided to Mr. Seselj in this case, that had been previously provided to assigned Defence counsel, were in the language of the accused. He told the registry that he refused to accept them because they had been provided to the assigned Defence counsel; that was his reasoning given at the time. And some of these materials were in hard copy, not in electronic form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to sum up, since we'll now have to have a break for technical reasons. As far as this matter is concerned, the situation is as follows. Mr. Seselj was informed of the fact that he had --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Antonetti, would you give me the floor for one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What Mr. Saxon has just said is not correct. I said nothing to the registry with regard to their letter; I ignored the letter. Each and every document which is in hard copy and in the Serbian language is a document that I will receive. Let me repeat this, but these documents should be provided to me. I can't say that I'll receive Hooper's state and check to see whether such documents are there. Any document that is marked as a Prosecution document or a registry document that's on hard copy in Serbian language, well, I'll receive such documents. What Mr. Saxon just said, his interpretation was erroneous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What you have said makes it easier for me to clarify what I wanted to clarify. The situation is as follows: The registry informed Mr. Seselj that there were 40 binders or boxes of documents at their disposal. Mr. Seselj says that given that these were documents from counsel Cooper, he didn't want to take charge of them because he never felt concerned by the fact that this person had been assigned as counsel. So he did not want to examine them. The Prosecution points out that among these documents, there are some in the Serbian language, documents from the Prosecution, that should be disclosed. So that is the situation. Perhaps there is a solution and Mr. Saxon could consider it. He could liaise with the registry, he could contact the registry, but there might be a problem concerning confidentiality. The solution should be as follows: The registry, given its powers, should select documents from these boxes that concern the work of counsel, keep them confidential naturally, and it should also select Prosecution documents that were translated into the Serbian language, documents that should be provided to Mr. Seselj. So the documents should be sorted in this manner. That would be the solution, and I'll ask the registry to consider this so that Mr. Seselj may have at his disposal documents from the Prosecution; documents that the Prosecution had provided counsel with. But there's another solution, and perhaps Mr. Saxon has found this solution himself. Since the Prosecution is familiar with these documents, you yourself could provide these documents to Mr. Seselj directly, and this would help us save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, perhaps one preliminary step, Your Honour, before a final decision is made as to how to proceed. I can only assume that assigned Defence counsel, as professional counsel, before they left their position here, I can only assume that they would have provided a list or an inventory of the material that they left behind. And it might be helpful if that inventory could be provided to the Chamber and to the Prosecution as well, so we can review exactly what the material is. If such an inventory does not exist, perhaps in their review process the registry could create one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Saxon, for that information. It will make it possible for the registry to solve the problem. It's half past 10.00. As I've already said for technical reasons, it's necessary to have a break. We will resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I shall continue discussing the motions. I would like us to go into private session for a moment because I shall touch on certain confidential motions about protection measures. I am sorry, but I'm forced to ask you to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Prosecution has sent us several motions which I'm going to discuss. There is one regarding Witness VS1051. The previous Chamber agreed that this witness should testify under pseudonym, but my understanding is that the Prosecution wishes to ask for fresh measures and closed session. Is that the case, Mr. Saxon, for Witness VS1051?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Seselj, in more general terms, when there are protective measures requested by the Prosecution or vice versa by the Defence, when you will be calling your witnesses, the parties may have objections for the witnesses of the Prosecution. If the Prosecution wishes to call witnesses under protective measures, you may not be in agreement. And in that case, when you have -- when you receive this motion, you may say that you agree or you disagree. And in that event, you have 14 days to take a position. So I just wanted to inform you about this possibility that you have regarding measures of protection. I'm going to go quickly because there's another witness VS017 who has also asked for protective measures, and this question was resolved on the 22nd of November, 2006, at a Status Conference, but following a decision of the Chamber of the 5th of January, 2007, the issue is still on the agenda. Regarding witness VS017, where do we stand? I would like to hear from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, to the best of the Prosecution's knowledge and belief, this witness will testify when he testifies in public session with -- without the use of any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then that matter is resolved. We can now go back into open session because what I am going to discuss does not require any private hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There have been motions regarding video-conferencing. Witness VS1141 and Witness VS053, these are witnesses -- I'm not going to go into the contents nor the reasons regarding these witnesses -- for the coming of these witnesses, but just with respect to -- to the video-conference, the Tribunal may organise video-conference hearings usually for medical reasons, the witness cannot be -- travel; and in that case this witness may be cross-examined directly by means of a video-conference. But it is up to the Trial Chamber to decide when the time comes because for a video-conference one has to find a date, everyone has to be available for that date, and so on. Therefore, this matter will be raised later by the Trial Chamber itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we come to the motions pursuant to Rule 94. I ask you, Mr. Seselj, to follow closely. There's a motion of the 28th of November, 2006, in which the Prosecution asked the Chamber to file judicial notice for the list 65 ter which were admitted into evidence during other cases in the Tribunal. These are exhibits connected to the Krajisnik and Milosevic cases, and the translation of those exhibits was completed and disclosed on the 9th of February, 2007. Mr. Seselj, by this motion, the Prosecution is asking the Chamber - not me, but the Trial Chamber as a whole - to admit into evidence exhibits which were admitted during the Krajisnik and Milosevic cases and trials. It is up to you to say whether you agree, whether you disagree, and the reasons for your possible disagreement. Therefore, this is something that you will have to do, together with your assistants. Normally you should have responded within 40-day delay, running from the date of the translation -- 14-day delay, and the translation was conveyed to you on the 9th of February. So in principle, your time has expired. In view of the circumstances, I will give you additional time to respond because you must respond. You cannot say anything if you like. If you don't respond, the Chamber may come to the conclusion that you agree or that you have nothing to say, and in that case the Chamber may admit those exhibits. If on the other hand you contest such a request, the Chamber will look into it. So I draw your attention to this motion which requires a response on your part. There's another motion of the 14th of July, 2006, when the Prosecution also requested judicial notice to be taken of the documents admitted in the Milosevic and Mrksic cases and Krajisnik. And these exhibits are contained in Annex A. And hereto the translation was sent to you on the 8th of September, 2006. Normally the time available has expired, but once again, in view of the circumstances, I will grant you additional time to respond to these motions. And the third motion was filed the 23rd of May, 2006, and in an attachment to this motion, you have a whole list of facts, an enormous number of them. I have the motion in front of me, and there you will find a list of all the facts. For your information, these are facts which were mentioned in judgements in the Brdjanin, Blagojevic, Galic, Kupreskic, Krnojelac, Krstic, Kunarac, Simic, Stakic, Strugar, Tadic, and Vasiljevic cases. And proceeding from that, the Prosecutor has filed a list and I will tell you the number of facts. There are exactly 418 of these facts relating to locations contained in the indictment and facts which may affect you. So here again, you should have given your position, saying that you agree with some of them, that you contest others, and so on. Because I wish to tell you, Mr. Seselj, if a Chamber takes judicial notice of these facts, what are the legal consequences? They are such that in the judgement, the Chamber, in its explanation, may rely on the facts which were admitted by another Chamber, which were adjudicated by another Chamber. I won't go into any detail, but I wish to draw your attention to look closely at all this, because you may be affected and you need to express your opinion about them. As you are defending yourself alone, you have the possibility to respond, but this is an -- entails an enormous amount of work. I move on, now, to other motions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Mr. Antonetti, respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead, Mr. Seselj. I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to the three questions that you have raised, perhaps it would be best for me to respond immediately, which I can do now. Regarding these two motions of the Prosecution regarding exhibits, my legal assistants are preparing our responses and they will be ready in a few days. And if you remember, Mr. Antonetti, I asked at the last Status Conference that I be given an extension of time for one month for all my delayed responses to the filings of the Prosecution. That deadline has still not expired. I filed 14 submissions regarding 14 different submissions by the Prosecution, and I will be completing this work by Monday or Tuesday next week, when I will be able to file all these responses. Of course, I oppose in principle the introduction of exhibits from other cases, but the Prosecution has only given me a list of exhibits. I would need to have the exhibits themselves if they are in written form, unless they are photographs or knives, pistols, guns, and other such instruments. So whatever is an exhibit that can be in paper form and in Serbian, I need to have them to be able to react to them because I cannot react on the basis of a list alone. As for adjudicated facts, this is something I have looked into in detail, and I asked the previous Trial Chamber to allow me to respond to them. The Pre-Trial Judge said 50 pages, and my response was about 100 pages. I'm not sure of that. I filed this twice, and twice the registry send these back to me because I overstepped the page limit. But this was roughly of the same size as the submission of the Prosecution. I had to explain why I disagreed with every single fact which they considered to be an adjudicated fact, and the previous Pre-Trial Judge would not allow it. This is an enormous amount of work invested in this. These were my responses compiled by legal advisors point by point, and I think this is a fundamental document, and it cannot be eliminated by simply referring to instructions about the lengths of submissions because this can rather be a recommendation than a legal rule that has to be observed strictly. So I will file this once again, and at a previous Status Conference I already orally expressed my disagreement and you can probably find this in the transcript from last summer's Status Conference, I think. I am not quite sure whether it was that date. So I challenge all this and soon you will receive my written response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we're clear as far as those three motions are concerned. I'll move on. There is also a motion that concerns the transcripts of the testimony of a witness in the Milosevic case. You testified on the first five -- 16th of September, 2005. The Prosecution wants to tender your testimony into evidence, and I note that the translation was provided to you on the 28th of March, 2007. I don't know what your position is. Do you agree or not? Can you clarify this for me immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll tell you what my position is immediately. I would have a legal basis to oppose that suggestion because the Prosecution didn't provide me with -- me with the entire text of my testimony, but only certain extracts. But in order to show that my approach is correct, that I'm treated with you and the Prosecution fairly, I must say that I received video-cassettes of my testimony at my own request. My advisors have transcribed the testimony and a book has been published on that testimony. So I won't insist on having everything provided to me in Serbian and in hard copies, and I won't object to this being tendered into evidence because I'm proud of my testimony. But I would like to be provided with a written explanation with regard to the Prosecution comments that were made in relation to some of the extracts from my testimony, and my advisors would soon state which arguments of the Prosecution we would like to oppose or refute based on that testimony. So I would accept the entire transcript being tendered into evidence, not just extracts. I won't insist on having everything on paper and in Serbian, not in this case, because I have the Serbian version of my testimony. I compiled this myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have taken note of what you have just said. *There are two other matters I'll deal with, two other motions, confidential ones. It's not necessary to go into private session. I won't provide the names of the motions, just the numbers. 036 and 1008 are the numbers of the witnesses concerned. They are now deceased. These are witnesses who testified, and the translation for number 36 was sent to you, and for witness 108 -- 1008, you were provided with the information on the 15th of March, 2007, and you also have to respond to this motion. I also need to deal with another motion. The Prosecution filed a motion to reconsider the Trial Chamber's decision of the 22nd of November, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this motion -- yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to interrupt the Chamber. If we may go back to Your Honour's previous comment. At line 20 of the current page of the transcript, you make a description regarding the two witnesses involved, about their present state. I'm wondering whether that could be redacted from the transcript because it might serve to identify these persons. Thank you. *JUDGE ANTONETTI: [Interpretation] Very well. You're quite right. Mr. Registrar, prepare an order to redact the reference to the fact that they were now deceased. I'll deal with the motion from the Prosecution dated the 1st of December, 2006 now, in which request is made for the Chamber to reconsider its decision dated the 22nd of November. Mr. Saxon, as far as this motion is concerned, could you provide me with any information?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently, you already responded. It -- it's about having admitted, pursuant to Rule 92 bis, certain documents and there are also confidential annexes to these documents. But if you are not in a position to respond right now, this can be dealt with subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe that the Prosecution has responded in the past months to the -- has made a more complete response to the Trial Chamber's order, Your Honour, I believe. I can't give you the exact date of our response, but it has been filed. It was a fairly lengthy filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'd like to draw Mr. Seselj's attention to the fact that there is this motion, but you'll be following this closely, too. I will now move on to a motion which was filed on the 26th of October, 2006. It concerns admission into evidence of a statement of Witness 1119, pursuant to Article 92 ter. The translation was provided on the 6th of November, 2006. Mr. Seselj hasn't yet responded. For Witness VS017, there was a motion for this written statement to be admitted pursuant to Rule 92 ter, and apparently the Prosecution, or rather, the previous Trial Chamber informed the Prosecution that this witness should be a viva voce witness. And I'm telling the Prosecution that they should be aware of this. Witness VS052 will no longer be called by the Prosecution. In a motion dated -- there are, in fact, a number of motions with corrigendums: The 6th of March, 2007; the 3rd of October, 2006; the 17th of October, 2006; and the 30th of November, 2006. Very briefly, the Prosecution is requesting that 32 transcripts be admitted into evidence, and there are 220 previous statements and five statements of people who are now deceased. It seems that the accused has responded to this. Yes, Mr. Seselj, do you remember this motion?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I have not fully responded. It concerns five Prosecution witnesses who have died in the meantime, and for each witness the Prosecution requested that previous statements and previous testimony be filed. The Prosecution has a possibility, according to Rule 92 quater, but under item 3(A) [as interpreted] it says that if the testimony is to prove some of the acts of the accused for which he has been charged in the indictment, well, this can be a reason for not accepting the admission of such evidence. I'll mention one of the witnesses, Milan Babic, you mentioned him a moment ago, the other four, as far as I can remember, are still protected witnesses, although some of them died a few years ago. For one of them, the Prosecution requested that the protective measures be removed so that his name could be publicly mentioned, but I think that this could be decided for all four of them. There is absolutely no reason to continue concealing their names. There was no reason while they were alive, but now the situation is such as it is. I object to having their testimony admitted. I'm saying this orally now for the sake of the record, because I'm officially objecting to this proposal, but to seriously respond to this motion, the Prosecution has to provide me with the transcripts because now the Prosecution is asking for the transcripts to be admitted. But there are no transcripts, or rather, the Prosecution has them, you have them, but I don't have them. I don't think a decision can be taken about this until I'm provided with the transcripts so that I can see for myself that they're not charging me with anything, because the Prosecution says they're talking about general circumstances, that they're not accusing me of anything, and so on. That concerns one of them who has also died. As you can see, none of these testimonies has been provided to me, none of the five testimonies, not a single previous statement has been provided to me. But I need to have the previous statements or the transcripts of testimony given in other cases. I need to know about their agreements with the Prosecution on the admission of guilt, because that's one of my main arguments to object to their testimony because when they're bargaining, they're bargaining. He suggests lying in turn for a lighter sentence. So that's my main argument if it's not possible for me cross-examine a dead person, and I don't think the Trial Chamber can take a decision until I have all those transcripts at my disposal. A minute ago, you said that it had been accepted that one of the statements should be filed to according Rule 92 bis. As far as I can remember, I never received such a decision. I don't know when the Trial Chamber accepted this. As far as I know, there are many motions pursuant to 92 bis, Rule 92 bis, and Rule 92 ter and Rule 92 quater but not a single decision has yet been taken, or at least I haven't been informed of any such decisions; I can't remember any of them. As a rule, I'm opposed to all such decisions. As far as some of the motions are concerned, I have already stated my position in writing, and in two or three days I will also state what my position is in writing on other motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I've identified two problems. The first one - I'm looking at the Prosecution now - the first one is that the accused seems to be saying that as far as the admission of transcripts is concerned and previous statements, he hasn't been provided with these documents in his language. So that's the first problem that the accused has raised. Mr. Saxon, perhaps you can respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. The only format that exists for providing the prior testimonies of witnesses in this Tribunal to an accused is the B/C/S audio format; in other words, a CD-ROM. We do not in this Tribunal produce B/C/S transcripts of witness testimony; and therefore, in each of these cases with respect to the motions that you have raised, we have provided it in electronic form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So here's another problem which has been clearly identified now. Mr. Saxon has informed us very precisely about the problem. At the Tribunal, the transcripts are made in English and in French. We don't have no B/C/S transcript; however, we do have a B/C/S audio-recording which is provided or can be provided on a CD-ROM. The accused is saying - and he has already said this before - he is saying that he wants to be able to read the documents themselves. So this is a real problem for the Trial Chamber. I have my own personal position, but it might not be shared by others. My position is no secret. I've already informed you of what my position is. In this case, the accused should have the translation of the CD in a hard copy and in his own language. But other Judges might not share my point of view. It's for the Trial Chamber to rule. I have taken note of Mr. Seselj's position and of Mr. Saxon's position. As far as the expert reports are concerned --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I take the floor again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, but I believe you have already informed us of your position, but you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly with regard to the previous issue, in order not to have to return to it later. The only way of being provided with these transcripts is to have an official translation from English or French. It's not sufficient to have just a translation. We need an official translation, and that's a guarantee of the preciseness of the translation. The Prosecution has to prove that it used the same resources for my criminal prosecution as it did for finding exculpatory material. The Prosecution has not been trying to prove this. It hasn't taken any steps to prove this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, you have told us of your position but you added something else which needs examination, because you said that you wanted a translation, an official translation. Let's take an example. There's a witness, let's say a Spanish witness, who says something. This is interpreted into English and into French in the course of the hearing and it's interpreted into B/C/S and this is recorded on the CD. You are provided with an audio-recording, but the translation, according to what you say, is just a translation of the interpretation, it's not an official translation. And I believe that in your opinion, an official translation should be a translation done by the translation services. That in fact is what you are trying to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Antonetti, at the beginning of the Status Conference, you, yourself, said that the reliability of simultaneous interpretation was 80 per cent. I need 100 per cent reliable translation, if we're talking about transcripts that are being admitted, transcripts from other cases. So I don't want a 20 per cent margin of error which results from the fact that simultaneous interpretation is used. This means that someone has to take the transcript in English or in French, which is an official transcript. They have to use the recording in Serbian language, make a comparison, and then have an official translation done. Because if I have the simultaneous interpretation on paper and it's only 80 per cent reliable, well what does that -- where does that leave me? There's a 20 per cent margin of error, so I need an official translation. The transcript is in French or English, the person translating it into Serbian consults the transcript, and recording of the testimony, of the cross-examination, et cetera, and then I'm provided with an official translation so that I can be a hundred per cent sure that this is all authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have understood what you have said a while ago, and now you have further explained that very clearly. Mr. Saxon, as far as this is concerned, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I simply want to clarify a point that I see in the transcript that perhaps could be interpreted more than one way. The accused is not provided with a translation of the prior testimony of witnesses in his language; the accused is provided with an audio-recording of the original testimony so he can listen to the original testimony in his own language. That's all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I shall move on now -- yes, Mr. Seselj. Yes, yes, I give you the floor again, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A component part of the testimony are the questions put to that witness, they are an inseparable part of the testimony, and the translation of those questions has to be authentic and a hundred per cent accurate. And I am underlining the importance of this. It's not just a question of the witness, what the witness said, if he testified in Serbian, but also what the Prosecutor asked him, what the Trial Chamber asked him, what the Defence counsel ask him, who may be speaking English, French, or who knows what language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Everyone has commented on this issue, which is now quite clear. But for the moment it doesn't have a solution. The expert reports now. There were several motions and I shall very quickly refer to them. One motion dated the 19th of February, 2007, but the accused did not have a translation, which explains why this has not been ruled upon. The expert Grujic dated the 14th of July, 2006, that is a motion -- the date of the motion. The translation was conveyed on the 13th of February, 2007, but again we come across the same problem and that is that this was given on a CD and Mr. Seselj wants to have the document in hard copy. Then the expert Tabeau, the same problem we have with him. The translation was disclosed on the 13th of February, 2007, but again in CD form. The expert Strinovic, motion dated the 13th of February, 2006 [as interpreted]. The translation was given in CD form on the 13th of February, the same position of Mr. Seselj. Then Stankovic, the 12th of July, 2006, a translation handed over on the 13th of February, 2007. No reaction by Mr. Seselj except for saying that he doesn't want to have CDs.
